claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy has higher mechanical strength than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
The quinary alloy has greater strain hardening than its quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
Increased local lattice distortion causes the proposed enhancement in strength and strain hardening.
Local lattice distortion is intrinsically greater in the quinary alloy than in all of its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
The quinary alloy's local lattice distortion increases dislocation pile-up.
The quinary alloy's local lattice distortion alters stacking-fault energy relative to the subset alloys.
The proposed distortion and stacking-fault-energy effects can increase deformation twinning.
The proposed distortion effects can promote dynamic strain aging.
Atomic-size and electronic interactions among the full set of five elements generate the proposed greater local lattice distortion.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary alloys will have lower yield strength.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the ternary alloys will have lower yield strength.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit reduced strain hardening.
The quaternary and ternary alloys may have greater ductility than the quinary baseline.
Greater dislocation pile-up, altered stacking-fault-energy signatures, or increased twinning are indicators of increased lattice distortion.
Chemical short-range order may contribute to the mechanical-property differences independently of lattice distortion.
